content.text: Termination provisions reviewed. Key points: Sanofi (our party) holds a broad convenience right; all RevMed termination rights are conditioned on cause.

input.quote: (i) Termination by Sanofi for Convenience. Sanofi may terminate this Agreement (A) in its entirety by providing [***] written notice of termination to RevMed or (B) on a country-by-country or Product-by-Product basis by providing [***] written notice of termination to RevMed
input.rationale: Section 12.2(a)(i) gives us (Sanofi) an express, unilateral termination-for-convenience right on written notice, exercisable in the entirety or on a country-by-country / Product-by-Product basis, which is the preferred position (customer convenience exit, partial termination included). RevMed has no corresponding convenience right: its termination rights are all for cause — material breach (12.2(b)), insolvency (12.2(c)), Sanofi's development of a Competing Product (12.2(d)) and Sanofi's cessation of development (12.2(e)) — so there is no vendor mid-term walk-away. No early-termination fee or penalty is imposed on us for a convenience termination; the exit consequences in 12.3(c) are a grant-back/transition package customary for a license and collaboration of this type, and RevMed in fact pays us post-termination royalties on Termination Products (12.3(c)(ii)C), which is favourable to us. Two sub-elements fall short of the model wording but are not material deviations here: the notice periods in 12.2(a)(i) are redacted ([***]) and so cannot be confirmed against the 30-day preferred figure, and there is no pro-rata refund of prepaid amounts — a concept with limited application to a milestone/profit-share collaboration rather than a prepaid subscription. We should confirm on the unredacted execution version that the convenience notice period is no longer than 90 days; subject to that, the clause sits at or above the preferred position and requires no redline.
